Particular Baptist
par-TIK-yoo-lar BAP-tist
noun phrase (tradition)
"Particular" denotes the doctrine of particular (definite) redemption — Christ died particularly for the elect — distinguishing this Calvinistic Baptist stream from the General Baptists, who held a general (universal) atonement. The label arose in 17th-century England to mark the Reformed wing of the early Baptist movement.

📖 Biblical Definition

Particular Baptists were the Calvinistic (Reformed) wing of the 17th-century English Baptist movement, distinguished from the General Baptists by their doctrine of particular (definite) redemption — that Christ died effectually for the elect, not generally for all without distinction. Emerging in London in the 1630s-40s from the Jacob-Lathrop-Jessey independent congregation, the Particular Baptists held the full Reformed soteriology of the Westminster tradition while practicing believer's baptism by immersion and congregational church government. Their first confession, the 1644 (revised 1646) First London Baptist Confession, was issued by seven London congregations to distinguish themselves from continental Anabaptist radicalism and to demonstrate their Reformed orthodoxy. Their crowning document, the 1677/1689 Second London Baptist Confession of Faith (the "1689"), deliberately followed the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration almost word-for-word except on baptism, church government, and the civil magistrate — demonstrating that the Particular Baptists stood squarely within the Reformed confessional tradition. Their leading lights included William Kiffin, Hanserd Knollys, Benjamin Keach, and Nehemiah Coxe. The tradition produced the great Particular Baptist preachers of later generations — John Gill, Andrew Fuller, William Carey (the father of modern missions), and ultimately Charles Spurgeon, who pastored a Particular Baptist congregation. The modern Reformed Baptist movement is the direct heir of the Particular Baptists, and the recovery of the 1689 Confession in the late 20th and early 21st centuries is a deliberate return to this heritage.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Calvinistic (Reformed) wing of the 17th-century English Baptist movement, named for the doctrine of particular redemption; authors of the 1644 and 1689 London Baptist Confessions; forebears of Gill, Fuller, Carey, and Spurgeon, and of the modern Reformed Baptist movement.

PARTICULAR BAPTIST, noun phrase. "Particular" = particular (definite) redemption, distinguishing this Calvinistic stream from the General (Arminian) Baptists.

The Reformed wing of the 17th-century English Baptist movement; emerged in London in the 1630s-40s.

Confessions: First London Baptist Confession (1644/1646); Second London Baptist Confession (1677/1689), following Westminster and Savoy almost word-for-word except on baptism, church government, and the magistrate.

Leading figures: William Kiffin, Hanserd Knollys, Benjamin Keach, Nehemiah Coxe; later John Gill, Andrew Fuller, William Carey, Charles Spurgeon.

Direct forebear of the modern Reformed Baptist movement and the 1689 confessional recovery.

📖 Key Scripture

John 10:14-15 — "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep."

Acts 2:41 — "Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls."

Ephesians 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love."

Romans 8:29-30 — "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son... Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Particular Baptist heritage is corrupted when Baptist history is rewritten to erase its Reformed-confessional roots, when the "particular" of particular redemption is forgotten so that modern Baptists assume Arminianism is the Baptist default, or when the tradition is claimed for revivalistic decisionism foreign to its confessional soul.

expand to see more

Confessional-amnesia rewriting. Much of modern Baptist self-understanding assumes that Baptists have always been broadly evangelical, anti-creedal, and soft-Arminian by default — so that Calvinistic Baptists appear to be a recent novelty or an aberration. The historical record is the reverse: the Particular Baptists were Calvinistic from their 1640s origin, confessional from their first decade, and self-consciously Reformed in issuing the 1689 to mirror Westminster. The recovery of the 1689 Confession is not the importation of Presbyterian theology into Baptist life; it is the recovery of the Baptists' own confessional heritage. The amnesia, not the recovery, is the novelty.

Decisionist-soul replacement. The Particular Baptist tradition held believer's baptism within a fully Reformed soteriology: regeneration precedes faith, election is unconditional, the atonement is definite, and the call is effectual. Modern revivalistic Baptist practice often retains the believer's-baptism form while replacing the Reformed soul with Finneyite decisionism — the altar call, the sinner's prayer, decisional regeneration. The Particular Baptists baptized those whom they had reason to believe the Spirit had regenerated; they did not manufacture decisions. To claim the Particular Baptist name while holding a decisionist soteriology is to keep the body and lose the spirit of the tradition.
